a: The oracle concerning Babylon
p: Each of the ten oracles in Isaiah 13–23 opens with massa', a word from 'lift': the KJV's 'burden'.
b: Massa' comes from nasa', 'to lift'. It can mean a load carried on the back (Numbers 4:15) or a message lifted up by the voice, a solemn pronouncement. The KJV chose the first sense ('The burden of Babylon'); most modern versions choose the second, and the Plain follows them with 'oracle', as in Proverbs 30:1. Jeremiah 23:33–40 plays on both senses: when people ask for 'the LORD's burden', the answer is that they are the burden. In Isaiah the word is a heading. It marks ten pieces: Babylon (13:1), Philistia (14:28), Moab (15:1), Damascus (17:1), Egypt (19:1), the wilderness of the sea (21:1), Dumah (21:11), Arabia (21:13), the Valley of Vision (22:1) and Tyre (23:1). The same headings return in 30:6 and in Nahum, Habakkuk, Zechariah and Malachi.
r: Proverbs 30:1; Jeremiah 23:33–40; 30:6; Nahum 1:1; Habakkuk 1:1; Zechariah 9:1; Malachi 1:1

a: Babylon
p: In Isaiah's day Babylon was a restless province of Assyria; a century later it was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem.
b: In the late 700s BC Babylon was not yet a great empire. It was an ancient and famous city under Assyrian rule, which rebelled again and again, most of all under the Chaldean chief Merodach-baladan, who sent envoys to Hezekiah (39:1). Sennacherib sacked it in 689 BC. After 626 BC a Chaldean dynasty made it the capital of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC; it fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC. The collection puts Babylon first and gives it two chapters, so that Babylon stands for every proud power raised against God. The oracle on Assyria (14:24–27) is tucked in after it. Whether the poem was first aimed at the Babylon of Isaiah's day or of the exile is debated (see the chapter page).

a: my consecrated ones
p: The attackers are 'consecrated': set apart for a holy war that the LORD himself is waging.
b: Mequddashai means 'those I have made holy'. Before battle, Israel's soldiers were consecrated, set apart by ritual for the LORD's war (Joshua 3:5; 1 Samuel 21:5). Jeremiah speaks of 'consecrating' war and nations against Babylon (Jeremiah 6:4; Jeremiah 51:27–28). The shock here is that foreign armies, the Medes of 13:17, are the LORD's holy troops. The same idea runs through Isaiah: Assyria is the rod of his anger (10:5), and Cyrus is his anointed (45:1). The nations do not know whom they serve.

a: The LORD of Armies is counting off
p: 'The LORD of Armies' usually names God's heavenly hosts; here he reviews a real army.
b: The verb paqad is the word for mustering troops and counting them (Numbers 1:3; 1 Samuel 15:4). Its subject is YHWH tseva'ot, 'the LORD of Armies', and its object is tseva' milchamah, 'an army for war'. Isaiah makes the title concrete: the God whose name means commander of hosts is on the hills calling the roll of the nations he has summoned. The roar of 'kingdoms ... gathering' is the din of a great coalition, as the Persian empire was, drawn from many peoples.
orig: יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת מְפַקֵּד צְבָא (YHWH tseva'ot mefaqqed tseva')

a: to ruin all the earth
p: 'Erets can mean 'land' or 'earth': the poem keeps moving between Babylon and the whole world.
b: The Hebrew 'erets can be a country ('the land') or the world ('the earth'). Older translations often read 'the land' of Babylon throughout 13:5–13. But the poem speaks of an army 'from the edge of the sky' (13:5), of 'the world' (tevel, 13:11), of the stars going dark (13:10) and the heavens shaking (13:13). The Plain reads 'earth' in these verses because the oracle frames Babylon's fall inside a cosmic day of the LORD. Babylon's name appears only in the frame (13:1, 19). Many scholars think a general poem on the day of the LORD was later applied to Babylon; others read the cosmic language as the usual poetic way of describing the fall of an empire.

a: the day of the LORD is close
p: The first time Isaiah uses the exact phrase. Joel 1:15 has the same words.
b: Isaiah 2:12 spoke of 'a day for the LORD of Armies'; here, for the first time in the book, is the full phrase yom YHWH, 'the day of the LORD'. Amos 5:18–20 shows that people once looked forward to it as the day God would defeat Israel's enemies; Amos turned it into a day of darkness for Israel too. In Isaiah 13 it falls on Babylon, and on the world's pride. Joel 1:15 repeats this verse almost word for word, including the pun on Shaddai (see the next note). The prophets use the phrase for many judgments in history (Ezekiel 30:3 for Egypt, Obadiah 15 for Edom), and the New Testament for the end (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10).
r: 2:12; Joel 1:15; Joel 2:1–11; Amos 5:18–20; Ezekiel 30:3; Obadiah 15; Zephaniah 1:7; Zephaniah 1:14–16; 1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Peter 3:10

a: like havoc from the Almighty
p: 'Like shod from Shaddai': ruin from the Ruiner, a sound English cannot keep.
b: The Hebrew keshod mishshaddai puts shod, 'devastation, havoc', beside Shaddai, the old divine name the Plain renders 'the Almighty'. The meaning of Shaddai is debated (perhaps 'the one of the mountain', perhaps 'the one of the breast'), but here the prophet plays on the verb shadad, 'to devastate', as if the name meant 'the Devastator'. The Greek translators of Isaiah dropped the name and wrote only 'ruin from God'. Joel 1:15 has the same pun.

a: they will writhe like a woman giving birth
p: The prophets' picture of sudden, inescapable agony; Jesus and Paul use it of the end.
b: A woman in labor cannot stop what has begun, and the pain comes in waves. The prophets use the picture for terror at the approach of judgment (21:3; 26:17; Jeremiah 6:24; Jeremiah 49:22; Jeremiah 50:43; Micah 4:9–10). The picture can also carry hope, since labor ends in birth (66:7–9). Jesus calls the troubles before the end 'the beginning of birth pains' (Matthew 24:8), and Paul says destruction will come on the careless 'as labor pains on a pregnant woman' (1 Thessalonians 5:3).

a: will not flash with light
t: Darkened sun and stars, in the Gospels and Revelation
p: Jesus' words on the end of the age join this verse with 34:4. Are the lights literal or a picture?
b: Jesus' warning about the end draws on this verse and on 34:4: 'the sun will turn dark, the moon will not shed its glow, the stars will fall from the sky' (Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24–25). Revelation's sixth seal uses the same images (Revelation 6:12–13), and so does Joel (Joel 2:10, 31; Joel 3:15). Readers divide over what the images mean. Many take them as the prophets' stock language for the collapse of a political order: here they describe the fall of Babylon, an event in history, and Ezekiel 32:7–8 uses them for Pharaoh. Others hold that they also point to a real disturbance of the heavens at the end of the age. Both groups agree that the darkening of the lights that rule day and night (Genesis 1:16) pictures creation itself undone by judgment.
r: 34:4; Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24–25; Revelation 6:12–13; Joel 2:10; Joel 2:31; Joel 3:15; Ezekiel 32:7–8; Amos 8:9; Genesis 1:16

a: constellations
p: The Hebrew is the plural of Kesil, the name of Orion: 'the stars and their Orions'.
b: Kesil is the constellation Orion (Job 9:9; Job 38:31; Amos 5:8). The plural kesilim, found only here, means the great star-pictures in general, so most versions write 'constellations'. The Greek translators kept the name: 'the stars of heaven and Orion and all the array of heaven'. Kesil is also the ordinary word for 'fool', but the verse uses it only as a star name.

a: gold from Ophir
p: Ophir's gold was the finest known. Where Ophir lay is still unknown.
b: Solomon's ships brought gold from Ophir (1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11), and 'gold of Ophir' became a byword for the best (Job 22:24; Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9). A pottery fragment found at Tell Qasile, near Tel Aviv, is labeled 'gold of Ophir for Beth-horon', so the name was used in trade and not only in poetry. Ophir has been placed in southwest Arabia, on the African coast of the Red Sea (the land the Egyptians called Punt), and in India; no site is agreed. The verse means that after the slaughter of the day of the LORD, survivors will be rarer than the rarest gold.
r: 1 Kings 9:28; 1 Kings 10:11; Job 22:24; Job 28:16; Psalm 45:9; Genesis 10:29

a: the Medes
p: A people of the Iranian highlands. Named here, and in 21:2, as Babylon's destroyers.
b: The Medes lived in the Zagros mountains east of Assyria. Assyrian kings raided them in Isaiah's day, and Israelites deported in 722 BC were settled 'in the towns of Media' (2 Kings 17:6). In 614–612 BC the Medes joined Babylon to destroy Assyria's capitals. About 550 BC Cyrus of Persia took over the Median kingdom, so the empire that conquered Babylon in 539 BC was a Persian-Median state: Daniel's 'Medes and Persians' (Daniel 5:28). Readers in the lens of history see this verse fulfilled in 539 BC; many critical scholars date the oracle to the 540s for that reason, while traditional readers take it as Isaiah's prediction. The Medes 'count silver as nothing': they cannot be bought off, as Hezekiah once bought off Assyria (2 Kings 18:14–16).
r: 21:2; 2 Kings 17:6; 2 Kings 18:14–16; Jeremiah 51:11; Jeremiah 51:28; Daniel 5:28; Daniel 6:8

a: the Chaldeans' proud splendor
p: Kasdim: tribes of southern Babylonia whose dynasty ruled Babylon from 626 BC.
b: The Kasdim were Aramaic-speaking tribes in the marshes of southern Mesopotamia. In Isaiah's day their chief, Merodach-baladan, twice made himself king of Babylon against Assyria (39:1). From 626 BC Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar, of Chaldean stock, made Babylon an empire, so 'the Chaldeans' became another name for the Babylonians (2 Kings 25; Habakkuk 1:6). In Daniel the word also names a class of learned men (Daniel 2:2). The Plain keeps 'the Chaldeans' wherever the Hebrew has it.

a: will end like Sodom and Gomorrah
p: The Bible's standard picture of total, final destruction.
b: The Hebrew mahpekhah, 'overturning', is the word used of Sodom and Gomorrah in Deuteronomy 29:23 and Amos 4:11: the LORD 'overthrew those cities and the whole plain' (Genesis 19:25). The comparison means destruction that leaves no one living and no one returning (13:20). Isaiah has already said that Jerusalem itself would have been like Sodom except for a few survivors (1:9). Jeremiah applies the same words to Babylon (Jeremiah 50:40) and to Edom (Jeremiah 49:18).
r: Genesis 19:24–25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Amos 4:11; 1:9–10; Jeremiah 49:18; Jeremiah 50:40; Zephaniah 2:9

a: It will sit empty forever
p: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC without a battle. It emptied slowly over the next five centuries.
b: Babylon was not destroyed in 539 BC. Cyrus entered it peacefully, and it remained a royal city under Persia. It revolted against Darius I and Xerxes, and Alexander the Great died there in 323 BC. Its decline began when Seleucus I founded Seleucia on the Tigris about 305 BC and moved people there. By the first century AD the Greek geographer Strabo could call it largely a desert. Readers who stress fulfillment point to this long decline and to the site's emptiness in later centuries; others note that the poem pictures a sudden overthrow (13:19), which did not happen, and read it as poetic judgment on an empire, not a timetable. Saddam Hussein's partial rebuilding of the palace in the 1980s is sometimes cited in popular debate on both sides.

a: goat-demons
p: Se'irim means 'hairy ones': goats, but also the goat-shaped spirits Israel was forbidden to worship.
b: Se'irim is the ordinary word for male goats, but in Leviticus 17:7 it names the 'goat idols' to which Israel must not sacrifice, and in 2 Chronicles 11:15 Jeroboam appoints priests for them. So it can mean real wild goats among the ruins or the goat-spirits people believed haunted waste places. The Greek translators wrote daimonia, 'demons', and rendered benot ya'anah and 'iyyim as 'sirens' and 'donkey-centaurs' (13:21–22); the KJV has 'satyrs'. The Plain reads 'goat-demons' because the list moves from animals to beings people feared, as in 34:14, where Lilith appears. Revelation draws on this scene when fallen Babylon becomes 'a home for demons' (Revelation 18:2).

a: owls
p: Several of the animal names here are rare and uncertain.
b: The words are vivid but hard to identify. Tsiyyim (13:21) are 'desert dwellers', wild animals or desert people. 'Ochim, found only here, may be 'howlers', perhaps owls (KJV 'doleful creatures'). Benot ya'anah are ostriches or eagle owls. In 13:22 'iyyim are 'howlers', probably hyenas or jackals, and tannim are jackals. The KJV read tannim as 'dragons', mixing it with tannin, the sea monster (27:1). The point of the list is clear even where the species is not: palaces become dens.

a: jackals
p: The KJV's 'dragons' comes from confusing tannim (jackals) with tannin (a sea monster).
b: Tannim, plural of tan, are jackals, the animals of ruins (34:13; 35:7; Jeremiah 9:11; Micah 1:8). Tannin is a different word: a great sea creature or dragon (27:1; 51:9; Genesis 1:21). The two look alike, and the KJV often printed 'dragons' for jackals (here and in 34:13; 35:7). Modern versions agree on 'jackals'.

a: Foreigners will join them
p: The ger, a foreigner living among Israel, will 'join' and 'cling to' the house of Jacob.
b: The ger is a foreigner who lives among Israel. Here such people do more than live nearby: they 'join' (nilwah) and 'cling' (nispechu) to Israel. The verb 'join' returns in 56:3, 6, where foreigners 'join themselves to the LORD', and in Esther 9:27 and Zechariah 2:11. This short promise (14:1–2) holds two ideas side by side that Isaiah keeps together through the book: the nations will come to Israel's God (2:2–4; 19:23–25), and the nations that oppressed Israel will be humbled before it (14:2; 49:22–23; 60:10–14).

a: and rule over their slave drivers
p: The 'slave drivers' are the nogsim of Exodus: Israel's slavery in Egypt reversed.
b: Nogesim is the word for Pharaoh's slave drivers (Exodus 3:7; Exodus 5:6), and 14:4 calls the king of Babylon himself 'the slave driver'. The promise is a new exodus: the people who were driven like slaves will rest (14:3, where 'rest' and 'heavy work' also echo Exodus) and their masters will serve them. Readers have found this hard beside 19:25 and 56:6–7. Many interpreters read it as the reversal of roles that the oppressed long for in poetry, not as a plan for slavery; others see a real hope of Israel's vindication over its oppressors, which later chapters soften into the nations serving God alongside Israel (61:5–6).

a: taunt
p: Mashal: a saying, a proverb, here a taunt. The poem is shaped like a lament for the dead.
b: Mashal covers proverbs, parables and bywords (see the note at Proverbs 1:1); here it is a taunt song, as in Micah 2:4 and Habakkuk 2:6. The poem begins with 'ekh, 'How!', the cry that opens laments for the dead (2 Samuel 1:19; Lamentations 1:1), and many of its lines fall into the limping rhythm of Hebrew funeral songs (a long line answered by a short one). So it is a mock dirge: the oppressed sing a funeral song over the tyrant, and their 'mourning' is joy. The whole earth, the trees and the dead join in (14:7–10).

a: the king of Babylon
p: The tyrant is never named. Candidates run from Sargon II of Assyria to Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus.
b: The poem names no king, and readers have filled the gap in several ways. Jewish tradition usually took him to be Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed the Temple (the Talmud, Pesachim 94a; Rashi), or Belshazzar. Some modern scholars, following H. L. Ginsberg, think the poem was first written about Sargon II of Assyria, who also called himself king of Babylon: Sargon was killed in battle in 705 BC and his body was never recovered, a scandal Assyrian texts discuss, which would explain the unburied corpse of 14:19–20. On that view the poem was later set under the Babylon heading. Others think of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, or read the king as a type of every tyrant. Traditional readers who hold Isaiah's authorship see a prediction of Babylon's last king. The text's silence lets the song be sung over any oppressor.

a: The cypresses too
p: Berosh names a tall evergreen. The Plain reads 'cypress' every time, in Isaiah and in Ezekiel.
b: The Hebrew berosh is a tall evergreen, and translators have rendered it cypress, juniper, fir or pine (the KJV has 'fir tree' here). The tree cannot be identified with certainty. This Plain reads 'cypress' for the word wherever it occurs in Isaiah (37:24; 41:19; 55:13; 60:13) and in Ezekiel (27:5; 31:8), so a reader following the tree from book to book sees the same English.
r: Isaiah 37:24; Isaiah 41:19; Isaiah 55:13; Isaiah 60:13; Ezekiel 27:5; Ezekiel 31:8

a: no woodcutter has climbed up to us
p: Assyrian and Babylonian kings boasted of felling the cedars of Lebanon for their palaces.
b: Mesopotamia had no great timber, so its kings sent expeditions to the Lebanon range and boasted of it in their inscriptions. Nebuchadnezzar's inscriptions at Wadi Brisa in Lebanon tell how he cut a road for the cedars. Sennacherib's boast is quoted in 37:24: 'I chopped down its tall cedars, / its choice cypresses' (2 Kings 19:23). The epic of Gilgamesh already told of a hero who killed the guardian of the cedar forest. The trees' joy is part of the taunt: even creation was a victim of the tyrant, and it rests now that he lies down.

a: Sheol down below is roused over you
p: The dead kings rise from their thrones to greet the newcomer. Is this teaching or satire?
b: This is the Hebrew Bible's most vivid scene of Sheol, the world of the dead. The shades of former kings sit on thrones, rise to meet the tyrant, and speak (14:9–10); his bed is maggots (14:11). Ezekiel 32:17–32 has a similar tour, with Egypt's dead. Readers differ on how much to draw from it. Some find here the belief that the dead live on as weak shadows, aware and able to speak. Others stress that it is a taunt song, a piece of satire, and that its point is the tyrant's humiliation, not a map of the afterlife. Both agree that in Sheol the great are made equal to everyone: 'So you are as feeble as we are!' (14:10).

a: the shades
p: Rephaim are the dead. The same word names an ancient race of giants and, at Ugarit, the royal dead.
b: Rephaim in poetry are the dead in Sheol, 'the shades' (26:14, 19; Psalm 88:10; Proverbs 2:18; Job 26:5). The same word names an ancient people of giants east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11) and the valley near Jerusalem in 17:5. At Ugarit the rpum were the deified dead kings of the dynasty, called on in a royal funeral text (KTU 1.161). The link fits this verse well: the rephaim here are former kings on their thrones.

a: all the he-goats of the earth
p: 'Attudim, 'he-goats', is a word for leaders: the rams who walk in front of the flock.
b: The male goat leads the flock, so 'attudim became a word for chiefs (Jeremiah 50:8; Zechariah 10:3, where the LORD will punish the 'leaders'). The Plain keeps the animal to show the earthy humor of the scene: the great bucks of the world, now ghosts, climb off their thrones to greet a new arrival.

a: Shining One, son of Dawn
t: Helel, Lucifer and the morning star
p: Helel means 'shining one', most likely the morning star (Venus). 'Lucifer' is the Latin translation, not a Hebrew name.
b: Helel, found only here, comes from halal, 'to shine'. 'Son of Dawn' (ben Shachar) points to the bright star that rises before the sun, the planet Venus. The Greek has heosphoros, 'bringer of dawn', and Jerome's Latin has lucifer, 'light-bearer', the ordinary Latin name for the morning star. The KJV printed 'Lucifer' as a proper name, and through it, and through the reading of this verse as Satan's fall (see the next note), Lucifer became a name of the devil. In the Hebrew it is a mocking title for a king who shone briefly and fell. The same Latin word names Christ in the church's Easter Proclamation (the Exsultet), and Jesus calls himself 'the bright Morning Star' (Revelation 22:16; 2 Peter 1:19). A minority reads helel as the imperative 'Howl!' (as in Zechariah 11:2); the parallel with 'son of Dawn' makes 'shining one' more likely.

a: How you have fallen from the heavens
t: The king of Babylon or the fall of Satan?
p: The poem is about a human king. Since the early church, many have also read it as the fall of Satan.
b: In context the speaker mocks 'the king of Babylon' (14:4), 'the man who set the earth shaking' (14:16), whose corpse lies unburied (14:19). The Talmud reads it of Nebuchadnezzar (Chagigah 13a). But Jewish writers also used its words for a rebel angel: in 2 Enoch 29:4–5 an angel plans to set his throne higher than the clouds and be equal to God's power, and in the Latin Life of Adam and Eve 15 the devil boasts that he will set his seat above the stars and be like the Most High. Church fathers, reading it beside Luke 10:18 and Revelation 12:9, took it of the devil's fall: Tertullian (Against Marcion 5.11, 5.17), Origen (First Principles 1.5.5), Gregory the Great; Aquinas cites 14:14 on the angels' pride. Calvin called that reading an error 'arisen from ignorance', and most modern commentators read it of a king. Some evangelicals see both: the king, and the spiritual power behind him (Ezekiel 28:11–19).

a: You are hacked down to the ground
t: A star-god who tried to climb too high
p: The poem borrows an old story: Helel, son of the dawn god Shachar, tries to take the highest throne and falls.
b: Several details come from the language of Canaan. At Ugarit Shachar ('Dawn') was a god, twin of Shalim ('Dusk') (KTU 1.23). 'El', 'the Mount of Meeting' and 'Zaphon' (14:13) are the high god, the gods' assembly and Baal's mountain there. In the Baal Cycle, when Baal dies, the god Athtar is set on Baal's throne on Zaphon, but his feet do not reach the footstool, so he comes down to rule the earth instead (KTU 1.6 I 53–65). A god hll, 'the shining one', father of the Kotharat (KTU 1.24), may lie behind the name Helel, but no story of a fall is told of him. Athtar, linked with the morning star, is the closest parallel to the plot; others compare the Greek Phaethon. Most scholars conclude that Isaiah used a story his hearers knew to mock a king, turning the myth into satire.

a: I will sit on the Mount of Meeting
p: 'The Mount of Meeting' on 'Zaphon' is the mountain where the gods met in Canaanite belief.
b: Har mo'ed is 'the mountain of assembly'; mo'ed is the same word as in 'the tent of meeting'. Ugaritic texts speak of the gods meeting in assembly, and they place Baal's palace on Mount Zaphon (Jebel al-Aqra, on the coast of Syria). The Hebrew tsafon also means 'north', so older versions wrote 'the sides of the north' (KJV). Psalm 48:2 takes the title away from Baal's mountain and gives it to Zion: 'Mount Zion, the heights of Zaphon' (Psalm 48:2). The king wants to sit in the council of the gods, above 'the stars of God', the heavenly host (Job 38:7).

a: I will make myself the Most High's equal
p: From Eden and Babel to the man of lawlessness, the Bible's pattern of reaching for God's place.
b: The king's five 'I will' boasts (14:13–14) end in the wish to be like 'Elyon, 'the Most High'. The Bible tells this story often: the serpent's promise 'you will be like God' (Genesis 3:5), the tower 'with its head in the heavens' (Genesis 11:4), the king of Tyre who says 'I am a god' (Ezekiel 28:2), the little horn that grows up to the host of heaven (Daniel 8:10–11), and the man of lawlessness who sets himself up as God (2 Thessalonians 2:4). Jesus warns Capernaum in words drawn from 14:13–15: it will not be lifted up to heaven but will go down to Hades (Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15). The answer is always the same: 'No! Down to Sheol you are thrust' (14:15).
r: Genesis 3:5; Genesis 11:4; Ezekiel 28:2; Daniel 8:10–11; 2 Thessalonians 2:4; Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15; Philippians 2:6–8

a: to the remote depths of the Pit
t: From the heights of Zaphon to the depths of the Pit
p: The same Hebrew phrase, 'the far recesses', describes both the top of the gods' mountain and the bottom of the grave.
b: The king wanted to sit in yarkete tsafon, 'the remote heights of Zaphon' (14:13). He lands in yarkete bor, 'the remote depths of the Pit'. The Plain uses 'remote' in both places to keep the echo. Bor, 'pit, cistern', is a common name for the grave and the underworld (Psalm 28:1; Psalm 88:4; Ezekiel 32:23).

a: like a branch nobody wants
p: Netser is the 'shoot' of Jesse in 11:1. Here the tyrant is a rejected one. Some read 'a miscarriage' instead.
b: Netser is a green shoot, the word used of the messianic 'shoot' from Jesse's stump (11:1, part 07-12). The king of Babylon is a shoot 'nobody wants' (nit'av, 'abhorred'), thrown out like a cut-off sucker. Some scholars change one letter and read nefel, 'a stillborn child' (Job 3:16; Psalm 58:8), which fits a corpse; the Greek has 'like a loathsome corpse'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew. Whether or not the poet intended it, readers of the whole book see the contrast between the two shoots: one cast out, one on whom the Spirit rests.

a: But you are thrown out, away from your tomb
p: For ancient kings, an unburied body was the final disgrace.
b: Kings built tombs to be honored after death (14:18; compare Shebna's tomb in 22:16). To lie unburied, food for animals, was the curse of curses (1 Kings 14:11; Jeremiah 22:19, of Jehoiakim; 2 Kings 9:35–37, of Jezebel; Deuteronomy 28:26). Assyrian treaties threaten it, and Assyrian kings boasted of digging up their enemies' bones. If the poem was first about Sargon II (see the note at 14:4), the line had a sharp edge: Assyrian scribes asked what sin had caused their king's body to be lost on the battlefield.

a: and cover the face of the world with cities
p: The last word is 'cities' in the Hebrew, 'wars' in the Greek; some scholars read 'ruins'.
b: The Hebrew ends with 'arim, 'cities': the tyrant's sons must not fill the earth with their building schemes, like the builders of Babel (Genesis 11:4). The Greek has 'wars', and some scholars suggest 'iyyim, 'heaps of ruins', or 'arim in the rare sense 'enemies' (1 Samuel 28:16). The Plain keeps 'cities'; the sense is the same either way: the dynasty must end before it remakes the world in its image.

a: the hedgehog
p: Qippod is probably the hedgehog or porcupine; older versions have a bird.
b: Qippod appears again with ruins in 34:11 and Zephaniah 2:14. The word's root means 'roll up', which suits the hedgehog. The KJV, following some ancient guesses, has 'the bittern', a marsh bird, which fits the 'reedy pools' of this verse. Babylon's site did become marshland when the canals were neglected.

a: The LORD of Armies has taken an oath
t: Assyria broken in the LORD's land
p: A short oracle on Assyria, probably from Sennacherib's invasion of 701 BC.
b: These four verses turn from Babylon to Assyria, the empire of Isaiah's own day. The promise that Assyria will be broken 'in my own land' and 'on my mountains' fits the events of 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army withdrew from Judah after the disaster of 37:36 (2 Kings 19:35). Its second half (14:25b) closely repeats 10:27a (see the next note). The theme is the LORD's plan ('etsah): nations make plans, but only his stands (8:10; 19:12, 17; 23:8–9; 46:10). Placed after the Babylon chapters, the oracle reminds readers that the LORD who broke Assyria can break Babylon.

a: Then his yoke will come off them
p: 14:25 repeats 10:27: the yoke lifted from the shoulder.
b: Isaiah 10:27 (part 07-12) has nearly the same words: on that day the Assyrian's load will be taken from 'your shoulder' and his yoke from 'your neck'. Here the pronouns shift: 'from them' and 'from his shoulder', meaning Israel's, which the Plain renders 'their shoulder'. The Great Isaiah Scroll smooths the shift with 'from you' and 'your shoulder'. The yoke is the image of tribute and forced labor (9:4; 47:6; Jeremiah 27:2; Jeremiah 28:10–14). The Plain renders the shared verb yasur 'slide off' in both places.

a: this is the hand stretched out over every nation
p: The refrain against Israel, 'his hand is still stretched out', now covers every nation.
b: Isaiah 5:25 and 9:12, 17, 21 end with the refrain 'his hand is still stretched out': the LORD's judgment on his own people is not finished. The same 'stretched out' hand is now held over all the nations, the theme of chapters 13–23. Behind it stands the exodus, where the LORD redeemed Israel 'with my arm stretched out and with great judgments' (Exodus 6:6) and stretched his hand over Egypt (Exodus 7:5).

a: In the year King Ahaz died
t: When was the oracle on Philistia?
p: Ahaz died about 716/715 BC (or 727/726, by another reckoning). The 'stick that beat you' is debated.
b: This is the only dated massa' in chapters 13–23 (the sign-act of chapter 20 is also dated), and its heading echoes 6:1, 'In the year King Uzziah died'. The year of Ahaz's death is debated: about 716/715 BC in one reckoning, about 727/726 in another. The Philistines are told not to rejoice that 'the stick that beat you is snapped'. If that stick is Assyria, the death of an Assyrian king is meant: Tiglath-pileser III died in 727 BC and Shalmaneser V in 722. If it is Judah, Ahaz's death may be meant, since Uzziah had crushed the Philistines (2 Chronicles 26:6) and the Philistines had raided Judah under Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:18). On either view the warning is that worse is coming from the same root. Assyria's later campaigns in Philistia (720 BC, and 712–711 BC against Ashdod, chapter 20) bore it out.

a: a flying burning serpent
p: Saraf, 'burning one', is the word for the seraphim of 6:2 and the snakes of the wilderness.
b: The Hebrew is saraf me'ofef, 'a flying saraf'. Saraf means 'burning one'. In Numbers 21:6 the LORD sends 'the burning snakes' among the people, and in Isaiah 6:2 the seraphim fly above the throne with six wings. The same flying serpent returns in 30:6 among the dangers of the desert road to Egypt. Egyptian art showed winged cobras (the uraeus) as royal guardians, and Herodotus reports flying snakes in Arabia. The line builds a ladder of threats: snake, then adder, then a winged fiery serpent. The Targum reads it of the Messiah: from the descendants of Jesse will come one who strikes like a serpent; on that reading Hezekiah's victory over the Philistines (2 Kings 18:8) is in view.

a: Smoke is rolling in from the north
p: Invaders reached Philistia from the north. 'No one lags behind': a disciplined army.
b: Assyria lay northeast of Philistia, but its armies came down the coast road, so they arrived 'from the north', as Babylon later did (Jeremiah 1:14; Jeremiah 47:2). The smoke is the smoke of burning towns, or the dust of a marching column. The last line praises the enemy's discipline: no straggler falls out of its ranks (compare 5:26–27). The Greek and the Great Isaiah Scroll read the last line differently, but the general sense holds.

a: The LORD laid Zion's foundations
p: Philistine envoys ask Judah to join a revolt. The answer is to trust the LORD who founded Zion.
b: The 'envoys of the nation' were probably Philistine ambassadors inviting Judah to join an alliance against Assyria, as the Ashdod rebels did about 713–711 BC (chapter 20); Assyrian records name Judah among the states Ashdod approached. Isaiah's reply is the heart of his politics: Judah's security is not in alliances but in the LORD who 'laid Zion's foundations'. The same image returns in 28:16, where the LORD lays a tested cornerstone in Zion, and in Psalm 87:1: 'What he founded stands on the holy mountains' (Psalm 87:1). The refuge is for 'the poor among his people', a phrase the book uses for those who trust God rather than power (25:4; 49:13).

a: The oracle concerning Moab
p: Most of the towns named in 15–16 also appear on King Mesha's stone, set up in Dibon about 840 BC.
b: Moab was the high plateau east of the Dead Sea, between the Arnon gorge and the Zered (Wadi el-Hesa), good land for sheep, grain and vines. In 1868 a stone was found at Dhiban, the Dibon of 15:2, on which King Mesha (2 Kings 3:4) boasts that his god Chemosh helped him win back land from Israel. The Mesha Stele names Dibon, Medeba, Nebo, Jahaz, Horonaim and Aroer, all places in Isaiah 15–16, and it shows Moabite as a language very close to Hebrew. The oracle gives no date. Moab was overrun by Assyria under Tiglath-pileser III, Sargon II and Sennacherib, and by Arab tribes later; 16:13–14 says the poem is an older word given a new deadline. Jeremiah 48 reuses much of it.
r: 2 Kings 3:4–27; Numbers 21:26–30; Jeremiah 48; Amos 2:1–3; Zephaniah 2:8–11; Ruth 1:1–4

a: Kir of Moab
p: Two of Moab's chief towns. Kir is usually identified with Kerak, a fortress on a high spur.
b: Ar was on or near the Arnon, so old a Moabite town that Deuteronomy uses it for the whole land (Deuteronomy 2:9; Numbers 21:28). Kir of Moab, called Kir-hareseth in 16:7 and 2 Kings 3:25 and Kir-heres in 16:11, is usually placed at el-Kerak, a natural fortress with a later Crusader castle, where Mesha held out against Israel. The repeated 'in a single night' means a surprise attack: the two great towns fall before anyone can react.

a: Dibon has climbed to the temple
t: 'The house': a temple or a town?
p: The Hebrew is 'He has gone up, the house, and Dibon'. Some read a town called Bayith.
b: The line is compressed: literally 'He has gone up, the house and Dibon, the high places, to weep.' Most versions take 'the house' (habbayit) as Moab's temple, probably of Chemosh, and Dibon as the people who climb to it. Others take Bayith as a town name, perhaps Beth-baal-meon or Beth-diblathaim, both on the Mesha Stele. The Greek has 'Dibon, where your altar is'. The sense is clear: the people go up to their shrines on the heights, not to worship in peace but to wail.

a: Every head is shaved bare
p: Shaved heads, clipped beards, sackcloth and wailing on the rooftops: the public rites of grief.
b: The mourning customs of 15:2–3 were shared across the region: shaving the head and beard, putting on sackcloth, wailing in the streets and on flat roofs, cutting the body (Jeremiah 48:37–38; Micah 1:16; Amos 8:10). At Ugarit the god El mourns Baal by gashing his cheeks and chin. Israel's law forbade some of these rites for its own people (Leviticus 19:27–28; Deuteronomy 14:1), but the prophets still describe Israelites doing them (22:12; Jeremiah 16:6). Here the whole land is a funeral.

a: My heart cries out for Moab
t: A real lament or a mocking one?
p: The speaker weeps for an old enemy (15:5; 16:9, 11). Is the grief real, or irony like the taunt of chapter 14?
b: Chapters 15–16 sound like a funeral song for Moab, and the speaker joins in: 'My heart cries out for Moab' (15:5), 'I soak you with my tears' (16:9), 'my stomach throbs over Moab' (16:11). Since 'I have silenced the shout' (16:10) is the LORD's voice, some readers hear God himself grieving. Many commentators (for example Oswalt and Childs) take the grief as real: the prophet and the LORD take no pleasure in Moab's ruin, even though Moab's pride deserves it (16:6). Others, such as Brian Jones, read the lament as irony, a mock dirge like 14:4–21, with Moab's pride the real target. Jeremiah's version (Jeremiah 48:31–36) keeps the weeping and adds a promise that Moab's fortunes will be restored (Jeremiah 48:47).

a: Eglath-shelishiyah
p: The KJV reads 'an heifer of three years old'. It is a place name, also in Jeremiah 48:34.
b: 'Eglat shelishiyah can be read 'a third heifer' or 'a three-year-old heifer', and the Greek and the KJV took it that way ('they shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old'). But it stands in a list of places on the refugees' road south toward Zoar at the southern end of the Dead Sea, and Jeremiah 48:34 uses it the same way. Modern versions treat it as a town name, perhaps 'Third Eglath', to tell it apart from another Eglath; its site is unknown.

a: the Wadi of the Poplars
p: Probably Moab's southern border stream, the Zered. The Greek read 'Arabs'.
b: Nachal ha'aravim can mean 'the wadi of the poplars' (or willows) or, with different vowels, 'the wadi of the Arabs'; the Greek chose the second. A wadi is a stream bed that flows only after rain. Refugees carrying what they can are crossing out of Moab, most likely over the Zered (Wadi el-Hesa) into Edom, the route south from Zoar. 'The Wadi of the Arabah' (Amos 6:14) may be the same stream.

a: a lion for the survivors of Moab
p: After the slaughter, a lion for the survivors: either real lions in an emptied land or an enemy king.
b: When a land is emptied, wild animals come back (2 Kings 17:25–26, lions in depopulated Samaria; Leviticus 26:22). The lion may also stand for a conqueror, as in Jeremiah 4:7 and 49:19, where Babylon's king comes 'like a lion'. The Targum says plainly that a king will come up with his army, and Rashi names Nebuchadnezzar. Either way, there will be no escape: those who survive the first blow meet a second (compare Amos 5:19).

a: Send the land's ruler a lamb
p: Moab paid its tribute in sheep. Now it is told to send it to Zion, the only safe place.
b: Moab was sheep country. 'Mesha, the king of Moab, was a sheep breeder. He would hand over to the king of Israel a hundred thousand lambs' (2 Kings 3:4). Here Moab's refugees are told to send that tribute to 'the land's ruler' on Mount Zion, Judah's king, and ask for protection. Sela ('the rock') may be es-Sela near Bozrah in Edom, or Petra; the refugees have fled south, and the lambs must go north 'by the desert road'. The Greek is very different here ('I will send as it were reptiles on the land'). The Targum reads the ruler as 'the Messiah of Israel', as reported by Chilton.

a: Bring advice; give a ruling.
p: Most read 16:3–4 as Moab's envoys pleading with Zion. Others hear Zion's advice to Moab.
b: The verbs are commands to a woman, probably Daughter Zion (16:1): 'bring', 'make your shadow', 'shelter', 'do not give away'. Most commentators hear Moab's envoys asking Jerusalem for asylum: cover us like the shade of night at noon; do not hand our runaways to the enemy. A few read it as Judah's counsel to Moab. The Hebrew written text has a plural 'bring' and the reading tradition (the Qere) a feminine singular; the sense is unchanged. The plea receives no stated answer; 16:6 turns to Moab's pride, perhaps as the reason the refuge is refused, and Jeremiah 48 drops the plea entirely.

a: Then by loyal love a throne will be made firm
p: In the middle of Moab's lament, a promise: a Davidic king who rules by loyal love and justice.
b: After the oppressor is gone (16:4), a throne is 'made firm' by hesed, 'loyal love', and its king sits in 'emet, 'faithfulness', 'in David's tent'. He searches out justice and hurries to do righteousness. This is the ideal king of 9:7 and 11:1–5, and of 32:1. 'David's tent' means his house or dynasty; Amos 9:11 promises to raise 'the fallen booth of David', which James applies to the gathering of the Gentiles (Acts 15:16–17). The Targum makes the king 'the Messiah of Israel' (reported by Chilton). Christian readers have seen Christ, whose kingdom on David's throne will have no end (Luke 1:32–33). Read in context, the promise also answers Moab's plea: refuge will be found under the just rule of David's line.

a: its proudness, its pride, its insolence
p: Four words from one Hebrew root pile up Moab's pride. Jeremiah 48:29 makes it six.
b: The verse heaps up ge'on, ge', ga'avato and ge'ono, all from the root g'h, 'to be high': 'pride, proud, his pride, his pride'. The Plain varies the English to keep the pile-up readable. Jeremiah 48:29 lengthens the list. Moab's pride was proverbial (25:10–11; Zephaniah 2:8–10). The last phrase, 'its boasting that rings false' (lo' khen baddav, 'his empty talk is not right'), may also mean 'his oracle-priests are not true', since baddim are false prophets in 44:25; the Greek has 'your divination'.
orig: גְּאוֹן ... גֵּא ... גַּאֲוָתוֹ ... גְאוֹנוֹ (ge'on ... ge' ... ga'avato ... ge'ono)

a: the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth
p: 'Ashishe are cakes of pressed raisins, foods of feasts and worship. Jeremiah 48:31 reads 'the men of Kir-heres'.
b: 'Ashishim are cakes of dried grapes, given out at festivals (2 Samuel 6:19) and linked with worship of other gods in Hosea 3:1. Moab was vine country (16:8–10), and its raisin cakes stand for the joy of harvest now lost. The KJV took the word as 'foundations'. Jeremiah's parallel has 'anshe, 'the men of Kir-heres' (Jeremiah 48:31), a change of a few letters; the Greek has 'those who live in Deseth'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew of Isaiah.
r: Jeremiah 48:31; 2 Samuel 6:19; Hosea 3:1; Song of Songs 2:5

a: whose red grapes once laid low the lords of nations
p: The Hebrew can mean 'the lords of nations struck down its vines' or 'its wine struck down the lords of nations'.
b: The line is ba'ale goyim halmu serukkeha. Hebrew word order allows either noun to be the subject. The KJV reads 'the lords of the heathen have broken down the principal plants thereof': enemy armies trampled the vines. The Plain follows many modern scholars in reading the vine as the subject: Sibmah's wine was so strong that it 'struck down', made drunk, the rulers who drank it (compare 28:1, where Ephraim's leaders are beaten down by wine). Either way, the vineyard's fame once spread to Jazer in the north, into the desert to the east, and 'across the sea', the Dead Sea, to the west. Soreq, 'choice red vine', is the vine of the song in 5:2.
orig: בַּעֲלֵי גוֹיִם הָלְמוּ שְׂרוּקֶּיהָ (ba'ale goyim halmu serukkeha)

a: for the harvest shout has fallen
p: Hedad is the treaders' shout at the winepress; it is also an army's battle cry.
b: Hedad is the rhythmic shout of men treading grapes (Jeremiah 25:30; Jeremiah 48:33). It is also a war cry (Jeremiah 51:14). The line 'the hedad has fallen on your summer fruit' carries both: the joyful shout of harvest has stopped, and the enemy's shout has fallen on the crop. 16:10 finishes the thought: 'I have silenced the shout.'

a: my stomach throbs over Moab
p: The Hebrew places grief in the 'insides'. The KJV has 'my bowels'.
b: Me'ay, 'my inner parts', is where Hebrew feels deep emotion: Jeremiah's anguish (Jeremiah 4:19), God's yearning for Ephraim (Jeremiah 31:20), a lover's longing (Song of Songs 5:4). The KJV kept 'my bowels shall sound like an harp for Moab'. English locates feeling in the heart; the Plain uses 'stomach', which keeps the physical sense of a gut that aches. The Greek word splanchna carries the same idea into the New Testament (Philippians 1:8; Luke 1:78).
r: 63:15; Jeremiah 4:19; Jeremiah 31:20; Jeremiah 48:36; Song of Songs 5:4; Philippians 1:8

a: he will get nowhere
p: Prayer to Chemosh at Moab's shrine cannot help. Mesha's stone mentions a high place he built for Chemosh.
b: Early in his inscription Mesha says: 'I made this high place for Chemosh in Qarhoh.' Moab's god Chemosh is named in Numbers 21:29, and Solomon built a high place for him near Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:7). In 2 Kings 3:27 Mesha, in his despair, offers his son on the wall. Here Moab 'wears himself out' going up to the shrine and praying, but no answer comes. The contrast is with 16:5 and 14:32: the true refuge is the throne in Zion.
r: 15:2; Numbers 21:29; 1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 3:27; Jeremiah 48:13; Jeremiah 48:35; 1 Kings 18:26–29

a: That was the word the LORD spoke long ago about Moab
t: An old oracle with a new deadline
p: 16:13–14 says the poem was spoken earlier and now gets a date: within three years.
b: This prose note treats 15:1–16:12 as an older word and adds a new one: 'But now'. Scholars of every school see here how prophecy was handed on and reapplied. Traditional readers take Isaiah to be reusing an oracle he had given earlier, or one by an earlier prophet, and dating its fulfillment for his own hearers. Critical scholars think a poem older than Isaiah was taken up and given a deadline, perhaps in Sargon's time (about 715 BC). In 1831 Ferdinand Hitzig even argued that the original was by Jonah son of Amittai (2 Kings 14:25), a guess few follow. Jeremiah 48 shows the same poem reused a century later, against Babylon's attack on Moab.

a: counted the way a hired man counts his years
t: The years of a hired worker
p: A hired man works exactly the years in his contract, not a day more: so 'exactly three years'.
b: A laborer hired by the year counts the time carefully, waiting for the end of his term (Job 7:1–2; Job 14:6; Deuteronomy 15:18). So 'three years, like the years of a hired worker' means three years precisely, with no extension. The same phrase gives Kedar a year in 21:16. If the date line comes from Isaiah, it may point to Sargon's campaign of 715 or 711 BC.

a: Damascus is taken away and is a city no more
p: Damascus and Israel had allied against Judah. Assyria took Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722.
b: About 734 BC Rezin of Damascus and Pekah of Israel (Ephraim) attacked Ahaz of Judah to force him into their anti-Assyrian alliance (7:1–9; 2 Kings 16:5). Isaiah told Ahaz that both kingdoms would soon be plundered (8:4). Tiglath-pileser III answered Ahaz's appeal: 'He went up to Damascus and seized it, took its people away captive to Kir, and killed Rezin' (2 Kings 16:9). Damascus lost its kings and became an Assyrian province, and Samaria fell ten years later. The city itself was later rebuilt and is one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities in the world. Historical readers see the oracle fulfilled in 732 BC, the end of Aram as a kingdom; some modern prophecy writers expect a future total destruction because the city still stands. Most commentators read 'a pile of rubble' as the usual strong language of judgment.

a: will be like the glory of the Israelites
p: Aram's remnant will share Israel's 'glory', which 17:4 says is shrinking to nothing.
b: The oracle about Damascus turns quickly to Ephraim, the northern kingdom of Israel, its ally (7:2). 'Fortified towns will cease in Ephraim', and Aram's survivors 'will be like the glory of the Israelites'. The comparison is ironic: Israel's glory is about to waste away (17:4). The two allies will share one fate. The Greek reads 'you are no better than the Israelites', which makes the irony plain.

a: in the Valley of Rephaim
t: Gleaners in the Valley of Rephaim
p: A fertile valley southwest of Jerusalem. After the harvest, only gleanings are left.
b: The Valley of Rephaim runs from Jerusalem toward Bethlehem; David fought the Philistines there (2 Samuel 5:18–22). Isaiah's Jerusalem hearers knew its fields. The law left the edges of fields and the leftover ears for the poor (Leviticus 19:9; Ruth 2:2). Israel will be like a field after the reapers and the gleaners have gone: almost nothing left. The olive image of 17:6 says the same, and 24:13 repeats it for the whole earth.

a: as when an olive tree is knocked with sticks
p: Olives were beaten down with poles; a few always stayed out of reach. A picture of the remnant.
b: At harvest, olive trees were beaten with long sticks (Deuteronomy 24:20, where the leftovers are 'for the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow'). A few olives always stay at the top, out of reach. Isaiah uses the picture twice (here and 24:13): judgment will be nearly total, but not quite. That is the doctrine of the remnant in an image, as in 1:9 and 6:13. The note of hope comes in the next verse: those few will turn to their Maker (17:7).

a: the Asherah poles and the incense altars
p: Asherah was a goddess and the wooden pole that stood for her; chammanim were small altars for incense.
b: Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess, consort of El at Ugarit; an asherah was a wooden pole or tree set up at a shrine as her symbol (Deuteronomy 16:21; 2 Kings 18:4). Inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud (about 800 BC) mention 'YHWH and his Asherah', which shows how some Israelites joined her to the LORD's worship. Chammanim are probably small incense altars (Leviticus 26:30; 2 Chronicles 14:5; 2 Chronicles 34:4); one has been found inscribed with the word at Palmyra. The verse sets them beside the altars as 'what his fingers made', the book's charge against all idols (2:8; 44:9–20).

a: the Rock where you shelter
p: An echo of the Song of Moses: Israel forgot the Rock who fathered it.
b: 'You have forgotten the God who rescues you ... the Rock' recalls Deuteronomy 32: 'You ignored the Rock who fathered you, / and forgot the God who went into labor with you' (Deuteronomy 32:18). The Rock is a favorite name of God in that song (Deuteronomy 32:4, 15, 31) and in the Psalms (Psalm 18:2; Psalm 62:2). Forgetting is not a lapse of memory but a turning away. The cure is the remembering of 17:7: looking again to the Maker.

a: So you plant your delightful plants
p: The quick-sprouting 'delightful plants' may be the potted gardens of a dying-and-rising god.
b: Nit'e na'amanim, 'plantings of pleasantness', may allude to a rite known in the Greek world as the 'gardens of Adonis': seeds sown in shallow pots that sprouted fast and withered fast, while women mourned the young god who died (Plato mentions such gardens in the Phaedrus). Na'aman, 'the pleasant one', was a title of Adonis, a god of Phoenician origin, and Ezekiel 8:14 shows women in the Temple weeping for Tammuz, a similar figure. 'A stranger's vine shoots' would then be plants for a foreign god. Verdict: the link is likely but not certain; even read plainly, the verses mock a people who plant fast-growing hopes and harvest only grief (17:11).

a: yet the harvest is gone
p: The vowels give ned, 'a heap'; the same letters read nad mean 'flees, is gone'.
b: The Masoretic vowels read ned qatsir, 'a heap is the harvest', which the KJV renders 'the harvest shall be a heap'. But a heap of grain would be a good harvest, which does not fit the verse. Most modern versions read the same letters as nad, 'flees, wanders off', and the Plain follows them: the crop vanishes on the day of sickness. Some keep ned and take it as a heap of ruin, a harvest wasted.

a: crashing like the crash of mighty waters
p: The nations roar like the chaos waters; God rebukes them, and they scatter like chaff.
b: The poem uses sound: hamon ... kahamot ... yehemayun, 'roar ... like the roaring ... they roar'. The raging sea is an old picture of the forces of chaos that God subdues (Psalm 93:3–4; Job 38:8–11), and the Psalms apply it to hostile nations (Psalm 46:2–6; Psalm 65:7). God 'scolds' them (ga'ar, 'rebuke'), the same word used when he rebukes the sea (Psalm 104:7; Nahum 1:4), as Jesus later rebukes the wind and waves (Mark 4:39). Many readers connect these three verses with Sennacherib's army in 701 BC, gone by morning (17:14; 37:36).
r: Psalm 46:2–6; Psalm 65:7; Psalm 93:3–4; Psalm 104:7; Nahum 1:4; Jeremiah 6:23; Mark 4:39; 29:5–8

a: When evening comes, look, there is panic
p: Terror at night, nothing left by dawn: the pattern of Jerusalem's rescue in 701 BC.
b: The story of Sennacherib's defeat follows this shape: 'It happened that night. The angel of the LORD went out and struck the camp of Assyria ... People rose early in the morning, and there they all were, dead bodies' (2 Kings 19:35; Isaiah 37:36). Psalm 46:5 says 'God helps her at the turning of the morning' (Psalm 46:5), and 29:5–8 pictures the nations attacking Zion vanishing like a dream. The last lines turn the scene into a principle: this is what comes to those who rob God's people.

a: the land of buzzing wings
p: Tsiltsal kenafayim may be insects (perhaps the tsetse fly), sails, or the clatter of an army.
b: Tsiltsal is a whirring or rattling sound; the same root gives 'cymbals' (2 Samuel 6:5) and a kind of locust (Deuteronomy 28:42). 'The land of buzzing wings' may refer to the insects of the upper Nile, perhaps the tsetse fly; many think of swarms. The Greek has 'land of ships' wings', that is, sails, which fits the boats of 18:2. Others hear the whirr of Cush's armies. The Plain keeps a sound word, 'buzzing', which leaves the options open.

a: that lies beyond the rivers of Cush
p: Cush (Nubia) ruled Egypt from about 728 to 656 BC and courted Judah against Assyria.
b: Cush is the land of the upper Nile, in modern Sudan, which the Greek calls Ethiopia (hence the KJV's 'Ethiopia'). About 728 BC its king Piye marched north and conquered Egypt; his successors, the 25th Dynasty (Shabaka, Shabataka and Taharqa, the Bible's Tirhakah), ruled as pharaohs until Assyria drove them out (663 BC). They were Assyria's great rivals, and they sent embassies to the small states of Palestine to build alliances. Tirhakah marched against Sennacherib in 701 BC (37:9). This chapter is probably Isaiah's answer to such envoys at Hezekiah's court: go home; the LORD will act in his own time (18:4–6).

a: Woe to
p: Hoy can be a cry of grief or threat, or a call for attention: 'Hey!'
b: Hoy usually opens a judgment, and the site renders it 'Woe to'. But it can also be a call to attention ('Ho, everyone who is thirsty', 55:1), and here the envoys of Cush are sent home with a message and their people end by bringing gifts to Zion (18:7). So several versions have 'Ah' here. The Plain keeps 'Woe to' as the site's term, since the chapter still warns of the LORD's pruning (18:5–6), but the word may be closer to 'Listen, land of buzzing wings'.

a: a nation stretched tall and polished smooth
t: Tall and smooth: praise, not insult
p: The KJV's 'scattered and peeled' misreads two words that describe a tall, handsome people.
b: Memushakh means 'drawn out', so 'tall', and morat means 'polished' or 'smooth', perhaps of glossy skin or of men without beards. Herodotus reports that the Ethiopians were said to be the tallest and most handsome of all people. The KJV's 'a nation scattered and peeled' took the words in a hostile sense that the Hebrew does not require. The rest of the line describes a feared and powerful nation, 'of power upon power' (qav-qav, a doubled word whose meaning is debated; the KJV has 'meted out'), whose land is cut by the Nile and its branches. The same description returns in 18:7, where this proud people brings gifts to Zion.

a: in reed boats on the face of the water
p: Light boats of bundled papyrus were used on the Nile and could carry envoys swiftly.
b: Gome' is papyrus, the reed of the Nile marshes; Moses' basket was made of it (Exodus 2:3). Egyptians bound papyrus stalks into light boats, shown in many tomb paintings, and Job 9:26 compares swift days to 'papyrus boats'. Here 'the sea' (yam) is the Nile, as in 19:5. Envoys from Cush travel down the Nile and on to Jerusalem; the prophet sends them back home.

a: I will keep still and look on from my place
p: God waits like summer heat and dew; then, at the right moment, he cuts the vine.
b: The LORD's answer to the envoys is that he is not in a hurry. He watches quietly, like the shimmering heat of noon or a dew cloud in harvest, both of which help the crop ripen. Then, just before the harvest, he cuts the shoots (18:5). Most readers take the vine as Assyria, cut down at the height of its success (compare 10:33–34). The lesson for Judah and Cush is Isaiah's constant one: salvation lies in returning and rest (30:15), and do not trust alliances (30:1–7; 31:1–3). Some read the stillness as God's patience with the nations before judgment.

a: Mount Zion
p: The feared nation of 18:2 comes to Zion with gifts: a picture of the nations' worship.
b: The envoys sent home in 18:2 return in 18:7, not as allies but as worshipers. In the Hebrew the tall people are themselves the gift (see the Variants), brought 'to the place of the name of the LORD of Armies, Mount Zion'. Psalm 68:31 has the same hope: 'Envoys will come from Egypt. / Cush will run to stretch out its hands to God' (Psalm 68:31). After Sennacherib's retreat, 'Many people kept bringing gifts for the LORD to Jerusalem' (2 Chronicles 32:23). Zephaniah 3:10 sees worshipers coming 'from beyond the rivers of Cush'. Christian readers have seen a first fulfillment in the Ethiopian official who came to worship in Jerusalem and was baptized on the road home (Acts 8:27–39).

a: The LORD rides a fast cloud
p: A title of Baal at Ugarit, 'rider of the clouds', claimed in Israel for the LORD alone.
b: At Ugarit the storm god Baal is called rkb 'rpt, 'rider of the clouds'. Israel's poets take the picture for the LORD: he rides the heavens (Deuteronomy 33:26), makes the clouds his chariot (Psalm 104:3) and flies on a cherub (Psalm 18:10). Psalm 68:4 may use the same title. Daniel sees a human figure coming with the clouds of heaven (Daniel 7:13), and Jesus applies that to himself (Matthew 26:64; Revelation 1:7). Here the LORD rides into Egypt as a conqueror, and the land's many gods shake before him, as in the exodus, when he judged 'all the gods of Egypt' (Exodus 12:12).
r: Deuteronomy 33:26; Psalm 18:10; Psalm 68:4; Psalm 104:3; Daniel 7:13; Matthew 26:64; Revelation 1:7; Exodus 12:12

a: town with town, kingdom with kingdom
p: In the 700s BC Egypt was split among rival dynasties until the kings of Cush united it.
b: During Isaiah's lifetime Egypt had no single ruler. Several dynasties held the Delta and Middle Egypt at once (the 22nd, 23rd and 24th Dynasties), and local princes ruled their own cities. The victory stela of Piye of Cush, about 728 BC, lists the kings and princes he had to defeat. 'Kingdom with kingdom' fits that situation exactly. Isaiah's point is that the empire Judah's politicians wanted as an ally (30:1–7; 31:1) was itself in chaos, its famous wisdom confused (19:3, 11–14).

a: the muttering spirits
p: 'Ittim, found only here, probably means 'ghosts', from an Akkadian word for the spirit of a dead person.
b: Egypt will turn to every kind of supernatural help: the 'worthless idols' ('elilim), the 'ittim, 'the ghosts of the dead' and 'the spirits that know things' (the site renders the last two pairs as in Leviticus 19:31 and Deuteronomy 18:11). 'Ittim appears only here; most scholars connect it with Akkadian etemmu, 'ghost'. The Plain's 'muttering spirits' follows the sense of 8:19, where people consult the dead 'who chirp and mutter'. The Greek has 'those who speak from the earth'. Egypt's magicians were famous (Exodus 7:11), but the LORD will 'swallow up' its plans.

a: and a strong king will rule them
p: Candidates include Piye of Cush, Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal of Assyria, and Persia's Cambyses.
b: The oracle does not name Egypt's 'harsh lord'. In Isaiah's lifetime the Kushite king Piye (about 728 BC) and his successor Shabaka (about 716 BC) conquered Egypt by force. Esarhaddon of Assyria took Memphis in 671 BC, and Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes in 663 BC (Nahum 3:8–10). Later still, Cambyses of Persia conquered Egypt in 525 BC, and Artaxerxes III in 343 BC. Readers in the history lens tend to choose the Assyrian conquest, which came within a generation of Isaiah. Others think the oracle was meant to cover all of them: the land that once enslaved Israel would itself be ruled by hard masters.

a: The water will drain from the sea
p: In Egypt the broad Nile could be called 'the sea'. Without its flood, Egypt dies.
b: Yam, 'sea', here means the Nile, as in 18:2 and Nahum 3:8, and Egyptian texts also call the great river 'sea'. Egypt's life depended on the Nile's yearly flood, which watered the fields and filled the canals. A failed flood meant famine, as in Joseph's seven lean years (Genesis 41). Verses 5–10 trace the disaster through the economy: canals, reeds, fields, fishermen, flax-workers, weavers and wage earners. The 'river' (ye'or, an Egyptian word) is always the Nile.

a: The people who comb the flax
p: Egyptian linen was famous across the ancient world. Without the Nile, no flax.
b: Flax grew in the Nile valley and was combed, spun and woven into fine white linen, which Egypt exported (Ezekiel 27:7; Proverbs 7:16). Joseph was dressed in it (Genesis 41:42). Egyptian tomb paintings show the stages of work, from pulling flax to weaving. The Greek names byssus, the finest linen. A dry Nile means no flax, no work and no trade.

a: Its weavers will be crushed
p: Shatoteha can mean 'its foundations' (its leaders) or 'its weavers'. The Greek supports 'workers'.
b: Shatoteha is usually 'its foundations', as in Psalm 11:3, which would mean the pillars of society, its leaders. But the line is set between flax-workers (19:9) and wage earners (19:10b), and a verb shatah, 'to weave', is known from related languages, so many scholars read 'its weavers'. The Plain follows that. The Greek has 'those who work them', which supports 'weavers'; its 'beer-makers' in the next line comes from reading sekher, 'wages', as shekhar, 'beer'.

a: The officials of Zoan are pure fools
t: Zoan, Memphis and the wisdom of Egypt
p: Zoan (Tanis) and Memphis were royal cities. Egypt was famous for its wise men and old books of instruction.
b: Zoan, called Tanis by the Greeks, was a royal city in the northeast Delta from about 1070 BC on (Numbers 13:22; Psalm 78:12). Memphis (Hebrew Noph, 19:13) was Egypt's ancient capital near modern Cairo. Egypt prized its wisdom: Solomon's wisdom is said to go 'beyond ... all Egypt's wisdom' (1 Kings 4:30), and Moses was trained in it (Acts 7:22). Egyptian scribes copied instructions said to come from ancient kings and sages, which fits the courtiers' boast, 'I come from a line of sages, from a line of kings of old'. Isaiah mocks it: the sages cannot even tell what the LORD has planned (19:12; compare 29:14 and 1 Corinthians 1:19–20).
r: Numbers 13:22; Psalm 78:12; Psalm 78:43; 1 Kings 4:30; Acts 7:22; 29:14; 1 Corinthians 1:19–20; 30:4

a: a spirit of twisted thinking
p: The LORD himself sends confusion, as in 29:10 and 1 Kings 22:22.
b: Ruach 'iv'im is 'a spirit of distortions', from 'avah, 'to bend, twist'. The LORD 'mixes' it into Egypt as one mixes wine (5:22), so the nation staggers like a drunk. The Bible several times says that God sends confusion on those who have chosen folly: a 'spirit of deep sleep' on Jerusalem's prophets (29:10), a lying spirit on Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:22), 'a powerful delusion' on those who refuse the truth (2 Thessalonians 2:11). Theologians debate how to state this; the text presents it as judgment on a wisdom that had already turned from God.

a: whether by head or tail
t: Head and tail, palm frond and rush
p: The same pair as in 9:14: high and low, the tallest and the lowliest plants.
b: In 9:14 the LORD cut off 'head and tail from Israel, the palm frond and the rush'; 9:15 explains: the head is the elder and leader, the tail the lying prophet. Here the same idiom means that no one in Egypt, from top to bottom, will be able to do anything useful. The palm frond is the high crown of the tree; the rush grows in the marsh.

a: the language of Canaan
p: The only place the Bible calls Hebrew 'the language of Canaan'. Jewish communities did settle in Egypt.
b: The prophecy imagines towns in Egypt where people speak Hebrew, called here by its geographical name, the language of the land of Canaan, and swear oaths in the LORD's name. Jewish settlers were in Egypt by Jeremiah's day (Jeremiah 44:1 names Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis and Upper Egypt), and in the 400s BC a Judean garrison at Elephantine, on the southern border, had its own temple of YHW, known from the Aramaic papyri found there. In Hellenistic times Alexandria had one of the largest Jewish communities in the world, which translated the Scriptures into Greek. 'Five towns' may be a round number for a few among many.

a: an altar in the heart of the land of Egypt
t: An altar in Egypt: Elephantine and Leontopolis
p: A Jewish priest built a temple in Egypt in the 100s BC and cited this verse to justify it.
b: Deuteronomy 12 allows sacrifice only at 'the place the LORD will choose', and Deuteronomy 16:22 forbids standing stones. Yet here the LORD has an altar in Egypt and a stone at its border, a witness like the altar of Joshua 22:26–28 or Jacob's pillar (Genesis 31:45). Two Jewish temples did stand in Egypt. The Elephantine temple was destroyed in 410 BC. About 160 BC the priest Onias IV, a refugee from Jerusalem, built a temple at Leontopolis in the Delta; Josephus reports that he cited this prophecy of Isaiah to Ptolemy VI (Antiquities 13.62–73; War 7.420–436). It stood until the Romans closed it in AD 73. The Mishnah rules that priests who served there could not serve in Jerusalem (Mishnah Menachot 13:10). Christian interpreters read the verse of the gospel and the church in Egypt; Jerome took it as worship of the true God spreading there.
r: Deuteronomy 12:5; Deuteronomy 16:22; Joshua 22:26–28; Genesis 28:18; Genesis 31:45; Malachi 1:11; John 4:21–24

a: he will send them someone to save them and fight for them
t: Egypt cries out like Israel did
p: The pattern of Exodus and Judges, cry, savior, rescue, now applied to Egypt itself.
b: The words are the exodus in reverse. In Egypt 'the Israelites sighed from their labor and cried out' (Exodus 2:23), and the LORD said, 'I have also seen how the Egyptians are squeezing them' (Exodus 3:9), using the word for 'oppressors' found here. In Judges the cycle runs: 'the Israelites cried out to the LORD. The LORD raised up a rescuer for them' (Judges 3:9). Now Egyptians cry out under oppressors, and the LORD sends them a savior. The Greek has 'a man who will save them'. Christian readers have often seen Christ here; historical readers think of a ruler who gave Egypt relief; others take it as the shape of God's dealing with any people who call on him.

a: So the LORD will reveal himself to Egypt
t: 'Egypt will know that I am the LORD'
p: In Exodus, Egypt learned who the LORD was through plagues. Here knowing leads to worship.
b: The refrain of the exodus story is 'Egypt will know that I am the LORD' (Exodus 7:5; Exodus 14:4, 18): the plagues and the sea forced Pharaoh to acknowledge the God he had defied. Isaiah 19:21–22 takes the same words further. Egypt comes to know the LORD and serves him with sacrifices, grain offerings and vows. The LORD 'strikes' (nagaf, the plague word of Exodus 12:23, 27) but also heals. Judgment is not the end of God's purpose for Egypt; it is a means to its turning.
r: Exodus 7:5; Exodus 14:4; Exodus 14:18; Exodus 12:23; Hosea 6:1; Deuteronomy 32:39

a: a highway will run from Egypt to Assyria
p: The road that armies marched becomes a road of worship. The highway is one of Isaiah's great images.
b: Egypt and Assyria were the two superpowers between which Israel and Judah were crushed; their armies marched up and down the coastal road. Isaiah imagines that road turned into a highway of peace, and the two enemies worshiping together. The highway image returns through the book: for the return of the exiles from Assyria (11:16), 'the Holy Way' through the desert (35:8), the way prepared for the LORD (40:3) and the road for the nations to Zion (62:10). The verb 'serve' ('avad) can mean 'worship', so the Plain has 'worship alongside Assyria'; the Greek, reading it as 'serve', has 'the Egyptians will be slaves to the Assyrians'.

a: Blessed is my people Egypt
p: Israel's own titles, 'my people', 'the work of my hands', 'my inheritance', are given to Egypt and Assyria.
b: Few verses in the prophets reach as far. 'My people' is what the LORD called Israel when he brought it out of Egypt (Exodus 3:7); 'the work of my hands' is Israel in 60:21 and 64:8; 'my inheritance' is Israel in Deuteronomy 9:26. Israel stands as 'a third' with its old enemies, 'a blessing at the center of the world', fulfilling the promise to Abraham: 'All the clans of the earth will find blessing in you' (Genesis 12:3). Ancient readers found it hard. The Greek reads 'my people who are in Egypt and among the Assyrians', the Jews of the dispersion. The Targum makes all three titles Israel's: the people the LORD brought out of Egypt, exiled to Assyria for their sins, and now restored. Christian readers see here the inclusion of the Gentiles (Ephesians 2:14–19; Galatians 3:8). Modern Jewish and Christian commentators alike treat the verse as a high point of the Bible's vision of the nations.
r: Exodus 3:7; 60:21; 64:8; Deuteronomy 9:26; Genesis 12:3; 2:2–4; 56:7; Zechariah 2:11; Ephesians 2:14–19; Galatians 3:8

a: Sargon king of Assyria
t: Sargon and the revolt of Ashdod
p: The only place the Bible names Sargon II (722–705 BC). His records describe this very campaign.
b: For centuries Sargon was known only from this verse, and scholars usually identified him with another Assyrian king. Then in 1843 Paul-Émile Botta found his palace at Khorsabad, north of Nineveh, with inscriptions describing the revolt of Ashdod. About 713 BC Ashdod's king plotted against Assyria; Sargon replaced him, and the people put up a usurper named Iamani, who sought help from Egypt and from neighbors (an Assyrian text names Judah, Edom and Moab). In 711 BC the Assyrian army took Ashdod, and Iamani fled to the border of Egypt and Cush. The king of Cush, named Shapataku in an inscription found at Tang-i Var in Iran, sent him back to Assyria in chains. That is the fate of trusting Egypt and Cush that Isaiah enacted (20:5–6).

a: and went about naked and barefoot
t: How naked, and for how long?
p: 'Arom can mean fully naked or stripped to an undergarment. Some medieval Jewish thinkers held it happened in a vision.
b: 'Arom can mean completely naked, but also 'stripped' of the outer garment, as Saul 'lay naked' among the prophets (1 Samuel 19:24) and Peter 'had nothing on' in the boat (John 21:7), where the Greek says 'naked'. Many commentators think Isaiah went about in a loincloth, dressed like a captive, since the point is the humiliation of prisoners of war (20:4). The three years may mean that he did it on and off as a sign, rather than without a break. Ibn Ezra and Maimonides (Guide of the Perplexed 2.46) held that such commands were carried out in prophetic vision, not in public, because they seemed unworthy of a prophet; most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take the act as real. Prophets used such sign-acts often (Jeremiah 13:1–11; Jeremiah 27:2; Ezekiel 4–5; Hosea 1).
r: 1 Samuel 19:24; Micah 1:8; John 21:7; Jeremiah 13:1–11; Jeremiah 27:2; Ezekiel 4:1–5:4; Hosea 1:2

a: a sign and an omen
p: 'Ot and mofet: the prophet's body, like his children's names (8:18), becomes a message.
b: 'Ot, 'sign', and mofet, 'wonder, omen', are paired in the exodus story for the plagues (Deuteronomy 6:22). In 8:18 Isaiah says that he and his children are 'signs and omens' in Israel, because of their names. Here his whole appearance is the sign. A mofet often points ahead to an event that will confirm it (1 Kings 13:3). This is the only extended sign-act Isaiah performs; Jeremiah and Ezekiel have many.

a: their backsides bare
p: Assyrian reliefs show prisoners led away barefoot and stripped. Shame was part of conquest.
b: Assyrian palace reliefs, such as the Lachish reliefs from Sennacherib's palace in Nineveh, show captives marched off barefoot, and other Assyrian reliefs show prisoners stripped or in neck ropes. Stripping prisoners humiliated them and marked them as property. Isaiah's sign is aimed at Judah's hope: the very Egyptians and Cushites they looked to will walk to Assyria that way. The phrase 'to Egypt's disgrace' uses 'ervah, 'nakedness', a word for shame.

a: whoever lives on this coastland
p: 'I means coast or island. Here it is the Philistine coast, and by implication Judah too.
b: 'I is a coastland or island (23:2, 6; 41:1). 'This coastland' is the strip of Philistine cities, Ashdod among them, and its neighbors. Their cry, 'And us? How will we get away?', is meant for Judah's ears. Hezekiah's court was tempted by the same alliances (30:1–7; 31:1–3), and Assyria's field commander would later mock Judah for leaning on Egypt, 'this crushed reed' (36:6).

a: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea
p: A riddle title for Babylon, in the marshy south of Mesopotamia that Assyrians called 'the Sealand'.
b: Several titles in chapters 21–22 are riddles drawn from a word inside the oracle: 'the wilderness' from 21:1b, 'Dumah' (silence) in 21:11, 'the Valley of Vision' from 22:5. 'The wilderness of the sea' is probably southern Babylonia, the marshes at the head of the Persian Gulf, which Assyrian texts call mat tamti, 'the Sealand'. Its Chaldean chiefs, Merodach-baladan among them (39:1), led Babylon's revolts against Assyria. Verse 9 confirms that the subject is Babylon. The Greek has only 'the vision of the wilderness'. The storm from the Negev pictures an army sweeping in out of the desert.

a: Up, Elam! Close in, Media!
p: Elam and Media attacked Babylon both in 539 BC, under Cyrus, and as Assyria's enemies in the 700s.
b: Most readers take the oracle of the fall of Babylon to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC: Elam (whose territory around Susa came under Persia) and Media march together, as in 13:17. But Babylon also 'fell' several times in Isaiah's own century. Sargon took it from Merodach-baladan in 710 BC, and Sennacherib sacked it in 689 BC, when Elam had been Babylon's ally, not its enemy. Seth Erlandsson and A. A. Macintosh argue for an Assyrian-period setting, in which Judah's hopes in Babylon as an anti-Assyrian partner (39:1–8) are dashed. The double-crosser of 21:2 recurs in 24:16 and 33:1.

a: So my insides are full of cramps
t: Why is the prophet in anguish?
p: He feels the horror of what he sees, or he grieves because Judah's hopes rested on Babylon.
b: It is surprising that the prophet suffers over Babylon's fall, which elsewhere is good news for the exiles (14:4; 48:20). Some read the anguish as the physical shock of a terrible vision, as Daniel was left sick after his (Daniel 8:27). Others, who date the oracle to Isaiah's century, think he mourns because Judah had pinned its hopes on Babylon as an ally against Assyria. The language of a woman in labor is common for terror in the face of judgment (13:8; Jeremiah 4:31).

a: Lay the table! Spread the carpets!
t: A feast on the night Babylon fell
p: Herodotus and Xenophon say Babylon fell during a festival. Daniel 5 tells of Belshazzar's feast that night.
b: The scene cuts from a banquet to a call to arms. Ancient historians report that Babylon fell to Cyrus while the city was feasting: Herodotus says the inner city did not know the outer parts had been taken because a festival was going on (Histories 1.191), and Xenophon has the Persians enter during a night of revelry (Cyropaedia 7.5). Daniel 5 sets Belshazzar's banquet on the night the city fell. 'Spread the carpets' renders tsafoh hatsafit, a rare phrase that may instead mean 'set the watch'. Oiling a leather shield kept it supple and made blows glance off (2 Samuel 1:21).

a: Go, set up a watchman
p: A watchman scans the horizon and reports. The prophets often describe their task this way.
b: City walls had watchmen who looked out for messengers or enemies and shouted what they saw (2 Samuel 18:24–27). The prophets take the role as a picture of their calling: Habakkuk takes his stand at the watchpost to see what the LORD will say (Habakkuk 2:1), and Ezekiel is appointed a watchman for Israel (Ezekiel 3:17; Ezekiel 33:7). Here the prophet seems to split into two figures, the one commanded and the lookout he posts, and the lookout reports back to him. The vision is described as a kind of watching that takes patience (21:8).

a: Then he cried out like a lion
p: The Hebrew has 'a lion'. The Great Isaiah Scroll has 'the seer', which many modern translations follow.
b: The Masoretic Text reads 'aryeh, 'a lion': the lookout 'cried out like a lion', a deep, loud call (compare Revelation 10:3), or 'cried, A lion!', naming what he saw. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) reads 'the seer' (haro'eh), with nearly the same letters, and many modern translations adopt it. The Plain keeps the Leningrad Codex, whose letters 4QIsa-a, the Greek and the Latin also support. The evidence is set out in the Variants for this verse.

a: Fallen! Fallen is Babylon!
p: Revelation takes up this cry for the fall of 'Babylon the Great', the city that opposes God.
b: Jeremiah 51:8 has a single 'fallen'; the doubled cry returns twice in Revelation: 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the Great, who made all the nations drink the wine of her passionate sexual sin' (Revelation 14:8), and 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the Great! She has become a home for demons' (Revelation 18:2), which also echoes Isaiah 13:21. For Revelation, Babylon is the great power that persecutes God's people, probably Rome in John's day. The smashing of idols in Isaiah 21:9 was not literally what happened in 539 BC: the Cyrus Cylinder says Cyrus honored Marduk and restored gods to their temples. The prophet speaks of the end of Babylon's gods as powers.

a: child of my threshing floor
p: Grain was beaten on a threshing floor. The prophet's own people have been crushed like grain.
b: On the threshing floor, stalks were beaten or run over with a sledge so the grain came loose, then the chaff was blown away. The image is common for a conquered people (41:15; Micah 4:13; Amos 1:3). 'You whom I have threshed' are the prophet's hearers, Judah or the exiles, who have suffered under Babylon. 'Child of my threshing floor' is literally 'son of my floor'. The news that Babylon has fallen is addressed to them as a comfort.

a: The oracle concerning Dumah
t: Dumah: a place, and a pun
p: Dumah was an oasis in north Arabia. The word also means 'silence', and its letters resemble 'Edom'.
b: Dumah was one of the sons of Ishmael (Genesis 25:14), and an oasis of that name, Dumat al-Jandal, lay in northern Arabia; Assyrian texts call it Adummatu. But the call comes 'from Seir', which is Edom's mountain country, and the Greek translates the title 'the oracle concerning Idumea', that is, Edom. Dumah also means 'silence' (Psalm 94:17; Psalm 115:17), and many readers think the title is a wordplay: Edom, the land that hears only silence in reply. The oracle is the shortest in the collection, two verses.

a: Someone is calling me from Seir:
p: Jewish teachers read the question of Israel waiting for redemption; a Christian hymn made it a carol of hope.
b: The question is how much of the night is left before morning. In the Jerusalem Talmud (Taanit 1:1) the call 'from Seir' is Israel in exile under Edom, a name the rabbis used for Rome, asking the watchman, God, when redemption will come; the answer 'morning arrives' is followed by a teaching that it will come when Israel repents, or keeps one Sabbath properly. In 1825 John Bowring wrote the hymn 'Watchman, Tell Us of the Night', in which the watchman sees the star of Christ's coming. The verse has become a common picture of waiting in the dark for God's dawn.

a: Turn around and come again
p: The verbs are Aramaic in form. 'Turn' (shuvu) can also mean 'repent'.
b: The watchman's answer is a riddle. 'Morning arrives, and the night too' may mean that relief will come but darkness will return, or that the end of the night is not yet known. The verbs 'ask' (tiv'ayun, be'ayu) and 'come' ('etayu) have Aramaic forms, fitting a message for Arabian or Edomite neighbors. Shuvu, 'turn back, come again', is the usual word for repentance, and Jewish interpretation took it that way: if you want an answer, return to God.
orig: אִם־תִּבְעָיוּן בְּעָיוּ שֻׁבוּ אֵתָיוּ ('im-tiv'ayun be'ayu shuvu 'etayu)

a: The oracle concerning Arabia
p: Oasis towns and tribes on the incense routes of north Arabia, attacked by Assyria and later by Babylon.
b: The title 'Arabia' (ba'rav) can also be read 'in the evening', a possible riddle like the others in this chapter. Dedan (modern al-'Ula) and Tema (Tayma) were oasis towns on the caravan routes that carried incense north from southern Arabia. Kedar was a strong tribal confederation (Genesis 25:13; Psalm 120:5).
