Assyrian kings from Tiglath-pileser III to Ashurbanipal fought Arab tribes and queens, and the Babylonian king Nabonidus later lived at Tema for about ten years (about 552–543 BC). Here refugees flee the sword and the oases are called to feed them.
r: Genesis 25:3; Genesis 25:13–15; Jeremiah 25:23–24; Jeremiah 49:28–33; Ezekiel 27:20–21; Psalm 120:5; 60:7

a: In one more year
p: The same formula as 16:14, with one year instead of three. The Isaiah Scroll has 'three years' here too.
b: The formula 'counted the way a hired man counts his years' appeared in 16:14 for Moab: an exact limit, not a day more. Here Kedar has 'one more year' in the Masoretic Text; the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran reads 'three years', perhaps assimilated to 16:14. These dated additions suggest that older oracles were reapplied with fresh deadlines. The 'archers' fit the Arab tribes, who were famous bowmen (Genesis 21:20).

a: The oracle concerning the Valley of Vision
t: The Valley of Vision is Jerusalem
p: The one oracle 'against the nations' aimed at Jerusalem. Readers date it to 701 BC, to 711, or to 586.
b: The title comes from 22:5, and the place is clearly Jerusalem, the city of David (22:9). Jerusalem stands on hills, but it is ringed by valleys (Hinnom and Kidron), and it was the place where the prophet received his visions. The Greek has 'the valley of Zion'. Placing Jerusalem among the nations is the point: God's city is judged like the others. Many date the oracle to 701 BC, when the city celebrated after Sennacherib withdrew (37:36–37) though the countryside had fallen; others to the preparations of 711 or 705–701; others see in 22:1–4 a picture of 586 BC, when the leaders fled and were caught (2 Kings 25:4–7).

a: they were tied up by the archers
t: By the bow, or without it?
p: Miqqeshet can mean 'by the bow' or 'without the bow', that is, without a fight.
b: The Hebrew miqqeshet 'ussaru is 'from a bow they were bound'. The preposition min can mean 'by' or 'away from, without'. Read the first way, the officers were captured by the enemy's archers, as the KJV and the Plain have it. Read the second way, they were taken without a single bowshot, which fits the charge of 22:2 that the dead were not killed in battle; several modern versions take it so. Both readings shame the leaders who ran.

a: my dear people
p: Bat 'ammi, literally 'daughter of my people', is a term of tender grief for the whole nation.
b: Bat 'ammi is literally 'the daughter of my people'. As with 'Daughter Zion', the 'daughter' is the people personified, not one woman. The phrase is used almost only in laments, by a prophet weeping for the nation's destruction: here first, and then many times in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 8:21; Jeremiah 9:1) and in Lamentations (Lamentations 2:11; Lamentations 4:10). The site renders it 'my dear people' to keep the tenderness without suggesting a single daughter. Isaiah refuses comfort while others are celebrating.

a: a day of uproar, of stamping feet, of panic
p: The Hebrew piles up words that sound alike: mehumah, mevusah, mevukhah; meqarqar qir.
b: The three nouns mehumah umevusah umevukhah ('uproar and trampling and confusion') begin and end alike, and the next line has meqarqar qir, 'battering a wall', which imitates the sound of a ram against stone. The Plain cannot keep the sound, but it keeps the run of short, heavy phrases. The last line is uncertain. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads meqarqar qodsho 'al hahar, 'tearing down his holy place on the mountain'. Many scholars read qir veshoa' as two peoples, Kir and Shoa (compare 22:6; Ezekiel 23:23): 'Kir and Shoa at the mountain'.
orig: מְהוּמָה וּמְבוּסָה וּמְבוּכָה ... מְקַרְקַר קִר (mehumah umevusah umevukhah ... meqarqar qir)

a: Elam lifted the quiver
p: Troops from Elam and Kir, far to the east, served in the Assyrian army.
b: Elam lay east of Babylonia, around Susa; Kir is an unknown place to which Assyria deported the Arameans of Damascus (2 Kings 16:9; Amos 1:5; Amos 9:7). In 701 BC Elam was Assyria's enemy, so some take the verse as evidence for a later date, but Assyrian armies included contingents from conquered peoples, and Elamite archers may have served in them. The point is that distant peoples were brought to Jerusalem's gates.

a: the weapons in the House of the Forest
p: Solomon's armory hall, named for its rows of cedar pillars.
b: 'He also built the House of the Forest of Lebanon' (1 Kings 7:2), a great hall with four rows of cedar pillars, like a forest of trees. Solomon hung gold shields in it (1 Kings 10:17), and by this time it served as an armory. When Judah's 'covering', its outer defenses, was stripped away, the city's leaders checked their weapons. Isaiah's charge is that they looked to weapons and walls but not to God (22:11).

a: you gathered the water of the Lower Pool
p: Hezekiah cut a tunnel to bring spring water inside the walls. The Siloam inscription records its cutting.
b: Verses 9–11 describe the preparations for siege that Kings and Chronicles credit to Hezekiah: 'how he made the pool and the channel and brought the water into the city' (2 Kings 20:20). He 'stopped up the upper outlet of the waters of Gihon and led them straight down, westward, to the City of David' (2 Chronicles 32:30), and 'rebuilt the whole wall where it was broken' (2 Chronicles 32:5). The tunnel, about 533 meters long, still runs under the City of David to the Siloam Pool; the Hebrew inscription found in it in 1880 describes how the two crews met. A radiometric study of the plaster dated it to about 700 BC. Nahman Avigad excavated a wall about seven meters thick, the 'Broad Wall', which runs over houses torn down to build it (compare 22:10).

a: But you never looked to the one who did all this
p: The charge of 17:7–8 turned on Jerusalem: they looked to their own works, not to the one who planned events.
b: In 17:7 'people will look to their Maker' instead of the altars their hands made. Here Jerusalem looks to its weapons, its pools and its walls, but not to God. 'The one who did all this' and 'shaped it long before' is the LORD, who planned the events from long ago (37:26; 25:1). Isaiah does not condemn the engineering as such; he condemns trust in it without turning to God. The same choice runs through chapters 30–31 and Hezekiah's prayer in chapter 37.

a: for tomorrow we die!
t: 'Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die'
p: Paul quotes the Greek of this line in 1 Corinthians 15:32: if the dead are not raised, why not?
b: The people, told to mourn, feast instead, either in despair or in defiance. Their slogan uses two bare infinitives in Hebrew, like a proverb. Paul quotes the Greek form of the line in 1 Corinthians 15:32: if there is no resurrection, this would be the only sensible way to live. Similar mottos are known from the Greek world and appear in Ecclesiastes' advice to eat and drink while one can (Ecclesiastes 2:24; Ecclesiastes 9:7), though there it is set within the fear of God. Isaiah calls the slogan a guilt that will not be wiped away (22:14).

a: there will be no atonement for this guilt of yours
p: The rabbis drew from this verse that some sins are fully atoned only by death.
b: The LORD's words are an oath: literally 'if this guilt is atoned for you until you die', with the curse left unspoken. The Babylonian Talmud (Yoma 86a) uses the verse in its teaching on degrees of atonement: for the gravest sins, such as profaning God's name, repentance, the Day of Atonement and suffering together do not fully atone, and death completes it. The Targum reads 'until you die the second death', a phrase that also appears in Revelation 20:14.

a: to Shebna, who is over the palace
p: The highest office at court, a kind of chief of staff. Shebna is the only person Isaiah attacks by name.
b: 'Who is over the house' was the title of the king's chief minister, who ran the royal household and controlled access to the king. Obadiah held it under Ahab (1 Kings 18:3), Jotham under his father Uzziah (2 Kings 15:5). Shebna is also called sokhen, 'steward', a word known from Phoenician and Ugaritic for a high official. In 701 BC Eliakim is over the palace and Shebna is 'the secretary' (36:3; 2 Kings 18:18), so the demotion predicted here may already have happened, though the exile of 22:17–18 is not recorded. Shebna's name is unusual and may be shortened from Shebanyahu; some think he was a foreigner, which might explain 'What family do you have here?'

a: that you have dug yourself a tomb here
t: A royal steward's tomb in Silwan
p: A tomb inscription in Silwan, across the Kidron from Jerusalem, names '...yahu, who is over the house'.
b: In 1870 Charles Clermont-Ganneau found inscriptions cut into the face of a rock tomb in the village of Silwan, on the slope facing the City of David; the main one was removed to the British Museum. Nahman Avigad deciphered it in 1953: 'This is [the tomb of] ...yahu, who is over the house. There is no silver or gold here, only [his bones] and the bones of his maid-servant with him. Cursed be the man who opens this.' The name is broken, and many scholars have suggested Shebanyahu, the full form of Shebna. The tomb is of the right period and type, cut high in the rock. The identification cannot be proved, but it shows the kind of monument Isaiah condemned.

a: my servant Eliakim son of Hilkiah
p: Eliakim ('God raises up') appears as Hezekiah's palace chief in 701 BC (36:3).
b: Eliakim son of Hilkiah is 'over the palace' when he goes out with Shebna the secretary and Joah the recorder to meet Assyria's field commander (36:3, 22; 2 Kings 18:18), and Hezekiah sends him to Isaiah (37:2). The LORD calls him 'my servant', a title of honor given to Moses, David and Isaiah himself (20:3). His name means 'God raises up'. Bullae (seal impressions) from Judah bear the names of other royal officials of the period, though none can be firmly tied to Eliakim.

a: a father to the people of Jerusalem
p: In the ancient Near East a senior official could be called 'father' of the people or of the king.
b: Joseph says that God 'has made me a father to Pharaoh, master of his whole house' (Genesis 45:8), and similar titles are known from Egypt and Mesopotamia for viziers and advisers. A good official cares for those under him as a father does, which is the opposite of Shebna, who built a monument to himself. The tunic and belt (sash) were the robes of the office, handed over at investiture, as Aaron's robes passed to Eleazar (Numbers 20:26–28).

a: I will lay the key of David's house on his shoulder
p: Revelation 3:7 applies the words to Christ. Matthew 16:19 gives Peter 'the keys of the kingdom of heaven'.
b: The steward held the key of the palace and decided who could come in to the king. Ancient keys could be large, carried on the shoulder or hung from a belt. The words are applied to Christ in Revelation 3:7, 'who holds the key of David. What he opens no one can shut, and what he shuts no one can open'. In Matthew 16:19 Jesus says to Peter, 'To you I will give the keys of the kingdom of heaven', with authority to bind and loose. Many interpreters see Isaiah 22 behind that saying, and the steward's office has been used in debates about Peter's authority (see Christian traditions). The Targum has 'the key of the sanctuary and the authority of the house of David'; the Greek has 'the glory of David'.

a: like a tent peg in solid ground
p: A peg (yated) held a tent or hung household goods on a wall. A family could hang everything on one man.
b: Yated is a tent peg, or a peg driven into a wall for hanging pots and tools (Ezekiel 15:3). Eliakim will be firmly fixed, and his whole family will lean on him. Later prophecy uses the peg as a picture of a leader: from Judah will come the cornerstone, the tent peg and the battle bow (Zechariah 10:4), which the Targum reads of the Messiah. But 22:24–25 turns the image: hang too much on one peg and it gives way. Many readers take 22:25 to mean that Eliakim too would fall, through nepotism; others think 22:25 refers back to Shebna.

a: the peg hammered into solid ground will work loose
p: The secure peg is Eliakim himself, overloaded by his family, or Shebna, or every official who thinks himself secure.
b: Eliakim was promised firm footing in 22:23; now 'the peg hammered into solid ground' comes loose. Most modern scholars think the verse was added after events: Eliakim's relatives hung on him for jobs and favors, and the house fell. Rashi and some others apply the falling peg to Shebna, whose position had seemed secure. Others take it as a general warning that no human office is permanent. Christian readers who apply 22:22 to Christ note that the type does not fit at every point; the key of David passes to one who will not fail.

a: The oracle concerning Tyre
p: Tyre stood on an island off the Lebanese coast. Assyria, Babylon and finally Alexander besieged it.
b: Tyre was the greatest Phoenician port, built on a rocky island and a mainland settlement facing it. Josephus, quoting the Phoenician historian Menander, says that Shalmaneser V besieged it for five years (Antiquities 9.283–287). Sennacherib's annals say Luli, king of Sidon, 'fled far overseas' in 701 BC, probably to Cyprus. Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years, about 585–572 BC (Josephus, Against Apion 1.156; Ezekiel 29:18). The island was finally taken by Alexander the Great in 332 BC, after he built a causeway to it (Curtius 4.2–4). Isaiah's oracle may have been reused for more than one of these.
r: Ezekiel 26:1–28:19; Ezekiel 29:18; Amos 1:9–10; Joel 3:4–8; Zechariah 9:2–4; 1 Kings 5:1–12

a: Howl, ships of Tarshish!
p: Tarshish was a far western port, probably in Spain. 'Ships of Tarshish' were the large ocean-going ships.
b: Tarshish was a distant source of silver, iron, tin and lead (Jeremiah 10:9; Ezekiel 27:12), often thought to be Tartessos in southern Spain, though Sardinia and other places have been suggested. Jonah tried to sail there to get as far from Nineveh as possible (Jonah 1:3). 'Ships of Tarshish' came to mean large long-distance trading ships (2:16; 1 Kings 10:22). The Greek translates 'ships of Carthage', the great Phoenician colony in North Africa. Cyprus is Hebrew Kittim, from the Phoenician town Kition on the island.

a: the grain of Shihor
p: An Egyptian name for a branch of the Nile. Phoenician ships carried Egypt's grain across the sea.
b: Shihor comes from Egyptian Pa-she-Hor, 'the waters of Horus', the easternmost branch of the Nile in the Delta (Joshua 13:3; Jeremiah 2:18). The parallel line names 'the Nile' itself. Egypt's grain surplus was famous, and Phoenician merchants shipped it around the eastern Mediterranean. Egypt therefore has reason to writhe at Tyre's fall (23:5): its trade partner is gone.

a: for the sea has spoken
p: The sea, Tyre's mother, speaks like a woman left childless. Sidon was Tyre's mother city.
b: Sidon was the older city; Genesis lists 'Canaan fathered Sidon, his firstborn' (Genesis 10:15). Here the sea, 'the fortress of the sea', speaks: it is as if it had never borne children, because its young men and women, the sailors and colonists of Phoenicia, are gone. Some take 'the fortress of the sea' as Tyre itself. The shame of a woman with no children is a common image of a ruined city (47:8–9; 54:1). Later 54:1 reverses it for Zion: 'Sing for joy, you barren one who has borne no child!'

a: far away to live as a foreigner
p: Tyre founded trading colonies across the Mediterranean, the greatest of them Carthage.
b: Tyre's traders went out as foreigners (gur, to live as a ger) in distant lands. Phoenician colonies were planted in Cyprus, North Africa, Sicily, Sardinia and Spain; Carthage was traditionally founded from Tyre in 814 BC, and Gades (Cadiz) even earlier. 'Founded in the far-off past' fits Tyre's claim to great age; Herodotus says the priests of Tyre told him the city had been founded 2,300 years before his visit (Histories 2.44). The line may also mean that Tyre's people will now flee abroad as refugees.

a: whose traders were the great names of the world
p: Revelation 18 takes up the picture of a city whose merchants were the world's great men.
b: Tyre 'handed out crowns': it set up kings in its colonies, and its merchant houses had princely power. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27) catalogs its trade with every nation. Revelation's lament over Babylon draws on both prophets: 'Your merchants were the important people of the world' (Revelation 18:23), and ship captains and sailors 'stood far away' as they watched it burn (Revelation 18:17). The word for 'traders' here is kena'aneha, literally 'its Canaanites' (see 23:11).

a: nothing holds you in any longer
t: No restraint, no belt, no harbor?
p: Mezach means 'belt' or 'girdle'. Translations guess 'restraint', 'strength' or 'harbor'.
b: Mezach appears elsewhere only as a belt or girdle (Psalm 109:19; Job 12:21, in a related form). The Plain takes it as what held Tarshish in ('nothing holds you in'): with Tyre gone, the colony is no longer bound to its mother city and can spread over its land like the Nile in flood. The KJV has 'strength'. Some modern versions conjecture 'harbor' or 'market', fitting the end of trade, but no Hebrew text supports that meaning. The Greek has 'ships no longer come from Carthage'.

a: The LORD issued his command about Canaan
p: The Phoenicians called themselves Canaanites. Because they traded, the word came to mean 'merchant'.
b: 'Canaan' here is Phoenicia, the coastland of Tyre and Sidon. The Phoenicians called themselves by that name, and centuries later Augustine reports that the country people around Carthage still answered 'Canaanites' when asked what they were (Unfinished Commentary on Romans 13). Because Canaanites were known as traders, kena'ani came to mean 'merchant' in Hebrew (Proverbs 31:24, where the capable wife 'hands over belts to the traders'; Job 41:6; Zephaniah 1:11).

a: this was the people that did not exist!
p: The verse is one of the most obscure in Isaiah. Some emend 'Chaldeans' to 'Canaanites' or 'Kittim'.
b: As it stands the Hebrew points to the land of the Chaldeans, Babylonia, as an example: 'this people was not; Assyria founded it for desert creatures', and then it was besieged and razed, which fits Sennacherib's destruction of Babylon in 689 BC. If even Babylon could be leveled, so can Tyre. Some read it the other way: the Chaldeans, now in power, will destroy Tyre. Others emend Kasdim to Kena'anim or Kittim, making the whole verse about Phoenicia. The Plain renders the Hebrew as it stands, with Assyria as the subject.

a: for seventy years, as long as one king lives
p: Seventy years was a conventional span of divine anger, used also of Babylon's rule and in an Assyrian text.
b: 'Seventy years' is a long human lifetime, 'as long as one king lives' (compare Psalm 90:10). Jeremiah gives Babylon's rule over the nations seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10). An inscription of Esarhaddon says that Marduk had decreed seventy years of desolation for Babylon, but then relented and turned the number over to make it eleven, a play on cuneiform numerals. So the number was a known way to describe a fixed period of divine anger. For Tyre, a city forgotten for a generation, then restored.
r: Psalm 90:10; Jeremiah 25:11–12; Jeremiah 29:10; Daniel 9:2; Zechariah 1:12; 2 Chronicles 36:21

a: like the prostitute in the song
p: Tyre's commerce is pictured as a prostitute's trade: selling herself to every buyer.
b: The prophet quotes, or composes, a street song about an aging prostitute who goes out again with her lyre so that people will remember her. The point is commercial, not sexual: Tyre will get back into trade with 'every kingdom of the world' (23:17). Nahum uses the same picture for Nineveh (Nahum 3:4), and Revelation for Babylon, with whom the merchants of the earth grew rich (Revelation 18:3). The image presents trade that is done only for profit, with no loyalty, as a kind of unfaithfulness.

a: set apart as holy to the LORD
p: The Law forbade a prostitute's fee in the temple. Here Tyre's 'fee' becomes an offering.
b: Deuteronomy 23:18 says, 'Do not bring a prostitute's fee or the price of a dog into the house of the LORD your God'. Here, surprisingly, Tyre's trade profits, called her 'fee', become 'holy to the LORD', feeding and clothing those who serve him. The prophecy points to a transformation of the nations' wealth (60:5–11; Haggai 2:7). After the exile the people of Sidon and Tyre were paid to bring cedar from Lebanon for the second temple (Ezra 3:7), and later Tyrians traded in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 13:16). Christian readers have seen here the conversion of Tyre: Acts 21:3–6 finds disciples there, and Tyre later became an important bishopric.
r: Deuteronomy 23:18; 60:5–11; 61:6; Haggai 2:7–8; Ezra 3:7; Nehemiah 13:16; Psalm 45:12; Acts 21:3–6
